title: CASE OF TANASE AND OTHERS v. ROMANIA
conclusion: Struck out of the list (Article 37-1 - Striking out applications)
summary:
In the case of Tanase and Others v. Romania, the applicants were Romanian nationals of Roma origin who lived in the village of Bolintin Deal, Giurgiu County. The case arose from a series of violent attacks against the Roma community following the killing of a non-Roma villager by a Roma individual on the night of 6–7 April 1991. In retaliation, over two thousand non-Roma residents, joined by local officials, burned and destroyed the applicants’ homes and belongings, forcing the entire Roma community to flee and leaving them homeless. When the Roma attempted to return a month later, further violence ensued, resulting in additional homes being burned and the community being denied access to the village, church, and cemetery. The applicants lost all their possessions and were forced to relocate multiple times, often without legal documentation of residence.

The applicants sought justice through the Romanian courts, but the criminal proceedings resulted in only suspended sentences for the perpetrators and limited compensation, which was further reduced due to alleged provocation. The courts also used derogatory language, referring to the applicants as “gypsies.” The European Court of Human Rights was prepared to examine violations of Articles 3, 6, 8, 13, and 14 of the Convention and Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, but the case was struck out after the Romanian government acknowledged these violations, offered substantial compensation, and committed to a range of general and individual measures to address discrimination and improve conditions for Roma in Bolintin Deal.

This case is significant as it highlights the systemic violence and discrimination faced by Roma communities in post-communist Romania, and it underscores the importance of both individual redress and broader structural reforms to protect Roma and Traveller rights under the European Convention on Human Rights.
